title: Cost, capacity, and spend control for AI systems
summary: This intermediate module teaches you to calculate unit cost, translate measured demand into capacity, forecast spend, and choose controls that balance financial limits with service reliability. After completing it, you can build and explain a provider-neutral cost and capacity plan instead of treating an invoice or budget as an unexplained total.
objectives: Calculate direct usage cost and cost per successful outcome from measured workload data.
Separate fixed, variable, shared, and avoidable costs so that a cost model does not hide important assumptions.
Calculate required capacity from peak demand, measured safe throughput, and an explicit headroom factor.
Forecast spend with documented workload and price assumptions while identifying environment-specific values as UNKNOWN.
Choose monitoring, alerting, budgeting, and enforcement controls appropriate to the consequence of exceeding a spend limit.
Explain how retries, rejected work, capacity headroom, and service objectives connect cost management to reliability.

sections.title: What this intermediate module assumes
paragraphs: This module is explicitly intermediate. It assumes that you can work with multiplication, division, percentages, averages, request rates, and basic monitoring concepts. It introduces the cost and capacity relationships needed here, so it does not assume prior knowledge of queueing theory, financial accounting, or any named provider.

Before this module, you may be able to read a usage total or budget. After it, you can turn measured demand, prices, successful outcomes, and load-test results into a documented cost and capacity plan. You can also distinguish an informative budget alert from a control that actually limits work.

Exact prices, billing units, discounts, quotas, and contract terms are environment-specific. They are UNKNOWN until established from the applicable agreement, rate schedule, and usage records. Do not substitute an example value for an unknown production value.

sections.title: Start with a measurable unit of work
paragraphs: A cost model needs a denominator. Depending on the system, useful denominators can include a request, completed document, resolved case, generated asset, evaluated candidate, or other outcome. The best denominator represents value delivered rather than activity alone.

Define a successful outcome before calculating unit cost. A request that failed, was rejected, timed out, produced an unusable result, or was discarded may still consume billable resources. Counting only submitted requests can therefore conceal the cost of unsuccessful work.

Use two related measures when possible. Direct usage cost per request equals direct usage spend divided by attempted requests. Total attributable cost per successful outcome equals all costs assigned to the workload divided by the number of successful outcomes. The second measure connects spend to delivered value, while the first helps diagnose technical consumption.

Record the measurement period, workload boundary, success definition, included cost categories, and allocation method beside each result. Without those definitions, two unit-cost figures can use the same label while measuring different things.

sections.title: Build a transparent cost model
paragraphs: Separate costs into categories before adding them. Variable costs change with measured usage. Fixed costs remain for the period even if workload volume changes within the relevant range. Shared costs support more than one workload and require a documented allocation rule. Avoidable costs are consumed without delivering the intended outcome, such as unnecessary duplicate work or repeated failed attempts.

For a simple usage tier with one rate, direct usage spend equals billable units divided by the rate denominator, multiplied by the rate. If different unit classes, tiers, or time periods have different rates, calculate each applicable segment separately and then add the results. A single blended rate is safe only when its derivation is documented and appropriate for the decision.

A practical period equation is: total attributable spend equals direct variable spend plus assigned fixed spend plus assigned shared spend plus other applicable charges or adjustments. Taxes, credits, discounts, and commitments must be handled according to the actual agreement. Their values and treatment are UNKNOWN when that agreement is not available.

Consider a hypothetical workload with 2,400,000 billable units in a period. The hypothetical rate is 0.24 currency units per 1,000 billable units, so direct usage spend is 2,400 times 0.24, or 576 currency units. If assigned fixed and shared costs total 192 currency units, total attributable spend is 768 currency units. If 100,000 attempts produce 96,000 successful outcomes, total attributable cost per successful outcome is 768 divided by 96,000, or 0.008 currency units. These numbers are teaching inputs, not market prices.

sections.title: Translate demand into capacity
paragraphs: Capacity is the amount of workload a system can handle while meeting its stated service objectives. A theoretical maximum is not the same as safe operating capacity. Safe throughput should be measured under representative conditions while observing latency, errors, and saturation. The monitoring guidance in the sources identifies latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as central signals.

For an online workload, choose a planning demand such as a measured peak request rate or a justified forecast. Measure the sustainable throughput of one deployable capacity unit under the required service objective. Then apply an explicit headroom factor for uncertainty and variation. Required capacity units equal the ceiling of planning demand multiplied by the headroom factor, divided by safe throughput per capacity unit.

Suppose a hypothetical workload has planning demand of 120 requests per second. Testing shows that one capacity unit safely handles 18 requests per second under the target latency and error conditions. With a headroom factor of 1.25, required capacity is the ceiling of 120 times 1.25 divided by 18. The result is the ceiling of 8.33, so the plan requires 9 capacity units.

Headroom is a stated risk choice, not free capacity. More headroom can improve tolerance for bursts or uncertainty but can increase provisioned cost. Less headroom can reduce provisioned cost but leaves less room for variation. Record why the factor was chosen and identify the condition that would trigger a revision.

Average demand alone is insufficient when demand varies materially. Review peaks, duration, request classes, latency distributions, errors, saturation, and backlog behavior. For batch work, the corresponding questions are how much work must finish, the completion deadline, and the measured amount of work each capacity unit completes within that interval.

sections.title: Forecast cost and capacity together
paragraphs: A spend forecast combines a workload forecast with the applicable cost model. Begin with workload drivers, convert them into attempted work and billable units, apply the relevant rates, and then add fixed and allocated shared costs. Keep the workload assumptions separate from price assumptions so that each can be changed independently.

Use scenarios when important inputs are uncertain. A lower, planning, and stress scenario can vary demand, success rate, retry rate, unit consumption, safe throughput, or price. Scenario labels do not make uncertain inputs factual. Mark an input UNKNOWN until measurement, a contract, or another authoritative record establishes it.

Capacity and spend forecasts must reconcile. If the capacity plan assumes nine continuously active units but the cost model includes only six, the models describe different systems. If the financial plan assumes demand will be rejected after a threshold, the capacity and service plans must account for those rejected requests.

Reforecast when actual demand, success rate, unit consumption, throughput, or applicable rates depart materially from the assumptions. The threshold for materiality is organization-specific and is UNKNOWN unless a governing policy defines it.

sections.title: Use layered spend controls
paragraphs: Spend visibility is the first layer. Meter the billable quantities and connect them to a workload, environment, request class, and outcome where feasible. Reconcile operational measurements with billing records because the system's technical counters and the bill may use different boundaries or timing.

A budget is a financial plan. An alert reports that observed or forecast spend has crossed a chosen condition. Neither one necessarily prevents additional work. Treating an alert as a hard limit is a control-design error unless a separate enforcement mechanism is explicitly connected to it.

Guardrails can include review requirements, usage envelopes, concurrency limits, request admission rules, and limits by workload or tenant. Enforcement can reject, delay, queue, degrade, or stop work, so each enforcement action needs a defined reliability and user impact. The overload guidance in the sources explains why accepting work beyond safe capacity can harm a service and why overload responses need deliberate design.

Use a control ladder. First measure and attribute spend. Next forecast and compare it with an approved envelope. Then warn owners early enough to act. Finally, enforce a limit only where the consequence of continued spending is greater than the consequence of delaying or rejecting work. Assign an owner, response time, escalation path, and recovery procedure to every alert or enforcement control.

Governance should make decisions traceable. Record the metric, threshold, scope, owner, intended action, exceptions, and review date. The risk-management source supports explicit governance, measurement, and management rather than relying on an undocumented control.

sections.title: Diagnose variance instead of guessing
paragraphs: When spend differs from plan, decompose the difference. Check workload volume, billable units per attempt, success rate, repeated attempts, capacity hours, allocation changes, applicable rates, fixed charges, credits, and timing. This turns a total variance into candidate causes that can be tested.

For example, spend can rise while successful outcomes remain flat if attempts increase but success rate falls. Cost per attempt may appear stable even though cost per successful outcome becomes worse. Looking at both measures reveals the difference.

Do not label a cost as waste solely because it did not produce an immediate successful outcome. Testing, safety checks, resilience capacity, and evaluation can be intentional. Classify a cost as avoidable only after comparing it with the workload's documented purpose and risk requirements.

Close the loop after a change. Verify whether spend, successful outcomes, latency, errors, and saturation moved as expected. A change that lowers unit cost but violates a service or quality objective is not an unconditional improvement.

sections.title: Run a repeatable operating review
paragraphs: A useful review begins with definitions: the workload boundary, successful outcome, service objective, measurement period, and cost categories. It then compares actual demand, capacity, spend, and unit cost with the plan. Variances are assigned to named causes only when evidence supports them.

The review should identify unknowns explicitly. Examples include an unconfirmed future rate, an unmeasured safe throughput, or an undocumented allocation rule. For each unknown, record what evidence would establish it, such as an applicable rate schedule, a representative load test, or an approved accounting policy.

Finish with decisions and verification dates. Typical decisions include revising the forecast, measuring a missing input, changing capacity, reducing unsuccessful work, or adjusting a control threshold. Recheck both financial and service outcomes after implementation.

questions.prompt: In the module's hypothetical cost example, what is the total attributable cost per successful outcome?
questions.explanation: Total attributable spend is 768 currency units and there are 96,000 successful outcomes. Dividing 768 by 96,000 gives 0.008 currency units per successful outcome.

questions.prompt: Planning demand is 120 requests per second, the headroom factor is 1.25, and safe throughput is 18 requests per second per capacity unit. How many capacity units does the module's formula require?
questions.explanation: Multiply 120 by 1.25, divide by 18, and round up. The result is the ceiling of 8.33, which is 9 capacity units.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a budget alert is correct according to the module?
choices: It necessarily stops new work when the budget is reached.
It reports a condition but does not necessarily prevent more work.
It proves that all recorded spend is avoidable.
It replaces the need to measure billable quantities.
questions.explanation: A budget alert provides information. Preventing additional work requires a separately designed and connected enforcement mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which denominator best supports a value-oriented unit-cost measure?
questions.explanation: Total attributable spend divided by successful outcomes connects cost to delivered value and exposes the effect of unsuccessful work.

questions.prompt: What should you do when the applicable production rate has not been established?
choices: Use the hypothetical rate as if it were contractual.
Choose a plausible market rate and present it as fact.
Mark the rate UNKNOWN until an applicable agreement or rate schedule establishes it.
Omit variable usage from every future cost model.
questions.explanation: The module requires environment-specific rates to be marked UNKNOWN until authoritative contractual or billing evidence establishes them.
